title: Modeling framework description
text: rtmbGMACS provides a framework with which to develop, test, and fit a size-structured population dynamics model, after which management reference points and related quantities can be determined, projections under different management and environmental conditions can be made, and other analyses conducted. While the framework provides many options from which to create a model, the following sections provide a “high-level” overview of the general workflow to create and run a rtmbGMACS model.

title: Population dynamics
text:
Population dynamics
The fundamental population quantity tracked through time is the vector of abundance by population category, denoted here as \(N(y,s)\), where \(y\) represents a model year, \(s\) represents a season within a year. If there are \(n_d\) population categories, then \(N(y,s)\) is a \(n_d \times 1\) column vector . The population state \(N\) at \((y,s)\) is propagated to the next time step \((y', s')\) (i.e. \((y,s+1)\) or \((y+1,s=1)\) depending on whether s is the last season in year y). In its most general form, this type of process can be represented as a first-order, inhomogeneous, ordinary matrix differential equation
\[ \frac{dN(t)}{dt} = A(t) \cdot N(t) + R'(t) \tag{1}\]
where \(A\) is a \(n_d \times n_d\) matrix and \(R'\) is a \(n_d \times 1\) column vector. If \(A\) and \(R'\) are constant over the integration interval, \(A\) is diagonalizable, invertible, and all eigenvalues have a negative real part, then the solution to Equation 1 is
\[N(t) = {U \cdot e^{D \cdot t} \cdot U^T} \cdot N(0) - A^{-1} \cdot R'  \tag{2}\]
where \(D\) is a diagonal \(n_d \times n_d\) matrix and \(U\) is a \(n_d \times n_d\) matrix such that \(U^T \cdot A \cdot U = D\) and \(A^{-1}\) is the matrix inverse of \(A\). This also yields a longterm equilibrium solution
\[ N(t\to\infty) = - A^{-1} \cdot R'  \tag{3}\]
Although Equation 2 provides the solution to Equation 1 under fairly general conditions for population dynamics, rtmbGMACS adopts the simpler approaches taken in the original GMACS, which rely on more specific conditions:

Recruitment happens instantaneously at the end of a season
molting, mortality, and growth happen instantaneously at the end of a season
fleet activities providing indices of abundance (i.e., surveys) are instantaneous at the end of a season
fishing mortality can be either continuous within a season or instantaneous (if the latter, it occurs at the end of a season)
natural mortality is continuous within a season

These conditions lead to the simplified discrete time solution
\[ N(y',s') = T(y,s) \cdot N(y,s) + R(y,s)  \tag{4}\]
where \(N(y',s')\) again represents the vector of population abundance at the start of the season following \((y,s)\), \(T(y,s)\) is a \(n_d \times n_d\) “transition matrix” encapsulating the effects of biological processes and fishing within the season time step \(\delta t_{s(y)}\) on population abundance and \(R(y,s)\) is a \(n_d \times 1\) column vector representing the recruitment of new individuals to the population at the end of the time step. The notation for the season time step \(\delta t_{s(y)}\) is used because the (user-specified) length of season s may vary with year y.
The five conditions on model processes imposed above lead to ambiguities with respect to the exact order in which the instantaneous processes (recruitment, growth, instantaneous fishing mortality, surveys) occur at the end of a season. To resolve this ambiguity, rtmbGMACS follows GMACS and allows the user to specify multiple “instantaneous” seasons with \(\delta t_{s(y)}=0\). The user can then define multiple instantaneous seasons and assign a single instantaneous process to each season in the order they choose. Multiple continuous seasons may also be defined, with the constraint that \(1 = \sum \delta t_{s(y)}\) for each year y. This leads to simplified equations for the results of the various processes:

recruitment:
\[ N(y',s') = N(y,s) + R(y,s)  \tag{5}\]
molting, maturity, and growth:
\[ N(y',s') = T_G(y,s) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{6}\]
surveys:
\[ N(y',s') = T_V(y,s) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{7}\]
instantaneous fishing mortality:
\[ N(y',s') = T_{IFM}(y,s) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{8}\]
continuous total mortality (natural and continuous fishing mortality): \[ N(y',s') = T_{CTM}(y,s) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{9}\]

where s now represents a different season for each process.
All of the transition matrices above are diagonal except for \(T_G\), which accounts for transitions due to molting, maturity, and growth between population categories as well as within them, whereas the diagonal matrices account only for changes within each category. Because surveys are assumed to have no affect on the population, \(T_V(y,s)\) above is simply the identity matrix.
The growth matrix \(T_G(y,s)\) may be decomposed into matrices representing its constituent processes in two ways:
\[ T_G(y,s) = T_{grw}(y,s) \cdot T_{mat}(y,s) \cdot T_{mlt}(y,s)  \tag{10}\]
or
\[ T_G(y,s) = T_{mat}(y,s) \cdot T_{grw}(y,s) \cdot T_{mlt}(y,s) \tag{11}\]
depending on whether the molt to maturity depends on pre-molt size (Equation 10) or post-molt size (Equation 11). The matrix \(T_{mlt}(y,s)\) is diagonal, with elements providing the probability of molting for a given population category. The matrices \(T_{mat}(y,s)\) and \(T_{grw}(y,s)\) are not diagonal but are generally sparse because many of the potential transitions between population categories cannot occur (e.g., mature \(\to\) immature, male \(\to\) female).
The instantaneous version of the fishing mortality matrix \(T_{IFM}(y,s)\) is
\[T_{IFM}(y,s) = \sum_f F^{IFM}_f(y,s)  \tag{12}\]
and the continuous version of total mortality (natural plus fishing mortality)
\[T_{TCM}(y,s) = M(y,s) \cdot \delta t_{s(y)} + \sum_f F^{CTM}_f(y,s)  \tag{13}\]
Somewhat analagous to the longterm equilibrium solution Equation 3, the longterm equilibrium solution for the population progression outlined above can be obtained by realizing that
\[N(y+1,s=1) = \{ \prod_{s''>s_{rec}} T(y,s'') \} \{ \prod_{s'<s_{rec}} T(y,s') \} \cdot N(y,s=1) + R(y,s_{rec}) \}\] which simplifies to
\[ N(y+1,s=1) = \prod_{s'} \{ T(y,s') \} \cdot N(y,s=1) \} + \prod_{s'>s_{rec}}\{ T(y,s') \} \cdot R(y,s_{rec}) \]
or (combining the first two \(\prod\) terms as \(T'\) and the last term by \(T''\))
\[ N(y+1,s=1) = T'(y) \cdot N(y,s=1) \} + T''(y) \cdot R(y,s_{rec}) \]
For a longterm equilibrium solution to exist, \(T'(y)\), \(T''(y)\), and \(R(y,s_{rec})\) must be independent of y and \(s_{rec}\) (and can thus be written as \(T'\), \(T''\), and \(R\)), from which the equilibrium solution \(\bar N\) is seen to be
\[ \bar N = -T'^{-1} \cdot \{ T'' \cdot R \}  \tag{14}\]
In practice, \(T'\), \(T''\), and \(R\) are typically obtained by averaging over (possibly different) time intervals.

title: Introduction
text:
rtmbGMACS, the RTMB version of the Generalized Assessment Model for Crustacean Stocks, is a general modeling framework based on (RTMB)[https://github.com/kaskr/RTMB] used to develop size-structured integrated stock assessment models for exploited crustacean stocks. The RTMB version is designed to supersede the original GMACS, which was based on the C++ templated auto-differentiation framework AD Model Builder. The principal motivating factors to develop rtmbGMACS are: 1) that AD Model Builder has reached the end of its development and is no longer actively support; 2) RTMB is now a mature product with a large and active user community; 3) it allows the inclusion of random effects more synthetically than ADMB does, and 4) RTMB models can be debugged, run, and analyzed all with the R “ecosystem” whereas workflows using the original GMACS involved compiling and running a C++ model, converting the output text file results to R objects, and then analyzing the converted results in R. Additionally, GMACS imposes structural constraints on models and data that can currently be fit in an assessment model (e.g., models are single-area single species, and can have at most two pseudo age classes). rtmbGMACS is designed to be more flexible, scalable, and incorporate more likelihood formulations in addition to, like the original GMACS, be useful for both data-limited and data-rich situations.
Models developed using rtmbGMACS (henceforth, “rtmbGMACS models” or just “models”) will allow the user to determine the impact of fishing and environmental conditions on both the historical and current abundance of an exploited population, to evaluate sustainable rates of removals (i.e., catches), and to project the impact of future fishing and climate variability on stock size.
rtmbGMACS models can incorporate multiple data types from a variety of sources (e..g. fishery catch data, survey indices) and determine optimal values for unknown model parameters by statistically fitting the data in the form of an integrated analysis [@maunder_review_2013; @punt_review_2013]. This approach allows various kinds of data with different (and sometimes incomplete) collection histories to provide complementary information about fished stocks. GMACS provides options to define a population sub-model that predicts biological dynamics (growth, maturity,fecundity, recruitment, molting) and stock size, an observation sub-model that predicts expected values for different kind of data (e.g. fishery and/or survey abundance indices, fisheries discard data, size composition data, …) given the population size and environmental conditions, and a statistical sub-model that quantifies goodness of fit and provides best-fitting parameter estimates and associated variances. The framework also provides options for determining management-related quantities such as \(B_{MSY}\), \(F_{MSY}\), and sustainable harvest levels under various exploitation and environmental scenarios, as well as the ability to project the population forward under different exploitation and environmental scenarios.

Change directory to the quarto subfolder of the local repository or source distribution

will create the manual website in a docssubfolder of the local repo or source distribution.

To re-render the local manual website (after, e.g., updating your local repository), simply delete the contents of the docs folder and re-run the steps above.

title: Fleet dynamics
text:
Fleet dynamics

Fishery dynamics

Continuous fishing mortality
For a season s in which continuous fishing mortality occurs, the change in population abundance due to natural and fishing mortality from (y,s) to the next season (y’,s’) is given by
\[ \frac{dN(t)}{dt} = -\{M(y,s) + \sum_f \{F'(f,y,s)\}\} \cdot N(t)  \tag{1}\]
where \(M(y,s)\) is a diagonal \(n_d \times n_d\) matrix providing the rate of natural mortality by population category and \(F'(f,y,s)\) is a diagonal \(n_d \times n_d\) matrix providing the instantaneous fishing mortality rate for fleet f by population category. Integrating Equation 1 from the initial condition \(N(0) = N(y,s)\) yields
\[ N(t) = e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot t} \cdot N(0)  \tag{2}\]
which, over the season length \(\delta t_s\), results in
\[ N(y',s') = e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot \delta t} \cdot N(y,s) \]
where \(Z'(y,s) = \{M(y,s) + \sum_f \{F'(f,y,s)\}\} \cdot \delta t_s\) is a diagonal matrix and \(e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot \delta t}\) is the diagonal matrix obtained by exponentiating the diagonal elements of \(-Z'(y,s) \cdot \delta t\).
For any fleet f, the instantaneous fishing mortality rate can be expressed as the sum of retained, \(F'_r(f,y,s)\), and discard, \(F'_d(f,y,s)\), catch mortality rates (both diagonal matrices). Let
\[F'_c(f,y,s) = f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \]
represent the capture rate by population category, where \(f'_c(f,y,s)\) denotes the fully-selected capture rate (a scalar) and \(sel(f,y,s)\) denotes the selectivity by population category (a diagonal matrix) for fleet f. The retained and discard catch mortality rates are, respectively,
\[ \begin{eqnarray} F'_r(f,y,s) &=& F'_c(f,y,s) \cdot ret(f,y,c) \\
                                &=& f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot ret(f,y,c) \end{eqnarray} \] and
\[ \begin{eqnarray} F'_d(f,y,s) &=& F'_c(f,y,s) \cdot (1-ret(f,y,s)) \cdot dmr(f,y,s) \\
                                &=& f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot (1-ret(f,y,c)) \cdot dmr(f,y,s) \end{eqnarray} \]
where \(dmr(f,y,s)\) is the discard or handling mortality rate (really a probability: it’s the fraction of discards that die as a direct result of being discarded).
Consequently, the total fishing mortality rate can be expressed as
\[F'(f,y,s) = f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot \{ret(f,y,c) + (1-ret(f,y,c)) \cdot dmr(f,y,s)\} \tag{3}\]
Let \(C_T(f,y,s)\) denote the total catch by fleet f in year y and season s. The instantaneous change in \(C_t\) can be represented as
\[\frac{dC_T(t)}{dt} = F'_c(f,y,s) \cdot N(t)\] where \(N(t)\) is given by Equation 2. Integrating over time and using Equation 2, one obtains
\[ \begin{eqnarray} C_T(t) &=& \int_0^t \{F'_c(f,y,s) \cdot N(t) \cot dt \} \\
          &=& \int_0^t \{f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot t} \cdot N(0) \cdot dt \} \\
          &=& f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot \{\int_0^t e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot t} dt \} \cdot N(0) \\
          &=& \frac{f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s)}{Z'(y,s)} \cdot (1-e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot t}) \cdot N(0) \\
    \end{eqnarray}\]
and thus the total capture abundance by fleet f in year y and season f is given by:
\[C_T(f,y,s) = \frac{f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s)}{Z'(y,s)} \cdot (1-e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot \delta t_s}) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{4}\]
Similar results can be obtained for retained catch abundance (mortality):
\[C_R(f,y,s) = \frac{f'_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot ret(f,y,s))}{Z'(y,s)} \cdot (1-e^{-Z'(y,s) \cdot \delta t_s}) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{5}\]
as well as discard abundance \(C_D(f,y,s)\) and discard mortality (abundance) \(C_DM(f,y,s)\), although both are more simply calculated using
\[C_D(f,y,s) = C_T(f,y,s) - C_R(f,y,s)  \tag{6}\]
\[C_DM(f,y,s) = dmr(f,y,s) \cdot C_D(f,y,s) \tag{7}\]


Instantaneous fishing mortality
The equations for an instantaneous fishery (i.e., occurring in a season with \(\delta t_s=0\)) can be obtained from those for continuous fishing mortality by taking the limits of Equations 2 and 4 as \(t \to 0\) and \(F'(f,y,s) \to \inf\) in such a manner that \(F(f,y,s) = F'(f,y,s) \cdot t\) remains finite, with the result that
\[ N(y',s') = e^{-Z(y,s)} \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{8}\]
\[C_T(f,y,s) = \frac{f_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s)}{Z(y,s)} \cdot (1-e^{-Z(y,s)}) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{9}\]
and
\[C_R(f,y,s) = \frac{f_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot ret(f,y,s))}{Z(y,s)} \cdot (1-e^{-Z(y,s)}) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{10}\]
where \(f_c(f,y,s)\) is the instantaneous fishing mortality counterpart to \(f'_c(f,y,s)\) and
\[ Z(y,s) = \sum_f F(f,y,s)\]
where
\[ F(f,y,s) = f_c(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot \{ret(f,y,s) + (1-ret(f,y,s)) \cdot dmr(f,y,s)\}  \tag{11}\]



Survey “dynamics”
“Survey” fleets provide relative indices of population abundance by population category, and so survey catch abundance, \(C_S(f,y,s)\) is simply proportional to population abundance (although the proportionality constant may depend population category):
\[ C_S(f,y,s) = q(f,y,s) \cdot sel(f,y,s) \cdot N(y,s)  \tag{12}\]
where \(q(f,y,s)\) is the “fully-selected” catchability (the proportionality constant when \(sel(f,y,s)\) is 1) and \(sel(f,y,s)\) is survey selectivity.

title: Model dimensions
text:
Model dimensions
rtmbGMACS provides a framework for developing size-structured population dynamics models to, fundamentally, predict changes population abundance (\(N\)) through time across several user-determined population categories (or “dimensions”). Consequently, individual size (z) is always a fundamental population dimension, but because all dimensions in rtmbGMACS are necessarily discrete, z actually represents a (user-defined) size interval (e.g., z-\(\delta z/2\) to z+\(\delta z/2\), where \(\delta z\) is the bin width). Other biological characteristics (e.g., sex, maturity state) can also be (optionally) implemented as population dimensions. “Standard” population dimension variables are listed in Table Table 1 and should be used when required, but additional dimensions may be defined, as well. Additionally, not all population dimension variables need to be included in a model.




Table 1: Names for “standard” population dimension variables. In addition to these, “y”, “s”, and “f” are reserved as year, season, and fleet variables, respectively.






variable
description

Time constitutes the second fundamental dimension; it is decomposed into years (y) and seasons within a year (s) to facilitate projecting the population forward through time. Population abundance N can thus be represented as \(N(y,s,d)\), where \(d\) represents the collection of biological categories used to describe the population at any one time. The expansion of \(d\) by y and s is referred to here as the model dimensions.
“Fleet” (f) constitutes the third fundamental model dimension, with f identifying a specific fishery or survey “fleet”. Fleet-related quantities tracked in a model include total catch abundance (\(C_T\)), retained (landed) catch abundance (\(C_R\)), total catch mortality (\(C_M\)), and index abundance (\(C_I\)) where all four quantities are indexed by f,y,s, and d. The expansion of the model dimensions \((y,s,d)\) by f is referred to here as the fleet dimensions.

Population dimension examples
Model dimensions can be easily defined using the tidyr::expand_grid function, as in the following example which creates a dataframe (dfrPopDims) defining a set of population dimensions that include two sexes (x), two maturity states (m), and several size bins (z) as in Table Table 2.

  dimsPop = c("sex","maturity","size")
  x = c("male","female");
  m = c("immature","mature")
  z = seq(from=45,to=60,by=5);
  dfrPopDims = tidyr::expand_grid(x,m,z) |> dplyr::mutate(rid=dplyr::row_number());
  cap = "Population dimensions dataframe with sex, maturity state, and size classes defined."
  kableExtra::kbl(dfrPopDims,col.names=c(dimsPop,"row_id"),booktabs=TRUE,caption=cap);

It is possible to define population dimensions using a “nested” approach, as in Table Table 4.

  dimsPop = c("region","sex","maturity","size");
  r = c("east","west");
  x = c("male","female");

BSAI crab examples
The following code chunks provide example code to create population dimensions for Tanner crab, Bristol Bay red king crab (“BBRKC”), Norton Sound red king crab (“NSRKC)”, and eastern Aleutian Islands golden king crab (“EAG”) models based on the 2026 BSAI stock assessments.
The Tanner crab assessment model includes two sexes, two maturity states (“immature”, “mature”), and two shell conditions (“new shell”, “old shell”) in its population dynamics model but, because immature crab are assumed to molt annually, no immature old shell crab occur and this population category could be eliminated as in the following code chunk and Table Table 7.

  dimsPop = c("sex","maturity","shell condition","size");
  x = c("male","female");         x = factor(x,levels=x);
  m = c("immature","mature");     m = factor(m,levels=m);
  c = c("new shell","old shell"); c = factor(c,levels=c);
  zc = seq(from=25,to=185,by=5);                    #--size bin cutpoints
  zb = (zc[2:length(zc)] + zc[1:(length(zc)-1)])/2; #--size bin centers
  mc = dplyr::bind_rows(list(m=m[1],c=c[1]),list(m=m[2],c=c)); # create dataframe with shell condition nested inside maturity
  dfrDimsP = tidyr::expand_grid(x,mc,zb) |>             #--create expanded dataframe
               dplyr::rename(z=zb) |>                   #--rename 'zb' column to canonical 'z'
               dplyr::mutate(rid=dplyr::row_number());  #--add row id column
  cap = "Tanner crab population dimensions dataframe. Only classes with size bins < 100 mm CW are shown."
  kableExtra::kbl(dfrDimsP |> dplyr::filter(z<100),col.names=c(dimsPop,"row_id"),booktabs=TRUE,caption=cap);
